topic: SHA-256 mining is a search for a hash below a target
hook: Bitcoin mining isn't solving a puzzle. It's a lottery with a target.

scenes.narration: Miners aren't doing clever maths. They run SHA-256 hashing and look for a block header hash below the network target.
If the hash is too high, the miner changes the nonce and tries again.
Difficulty sets how low the hash must be, and it is recalculated every 2,016 blocks.
A lower target means a rarer winning hash, so more attempts are needed on average.

title: Bitcoin Mining Is a Lottery, Not a Puzzle
description_body: Miners repeatedly hash a block header and look for a result below the network target. Difficulty sets that target.

topic: What a block header holds: the previous hash and the merkle root
hook: Bitcoin miners don't hash the whole block. Just 80 bytes.

scenes.narration: Here is the surprise. Miners only run proof of work on the 80-byte block header.
That header holds the previous block's hash, which links the chain together, plus the merkle root of the block's transactions.
It also has a nonce, an easy field to change, so miners can try fresh hashes over and over.
Every attempt changes only that tiny nonce, and the header is hashed again.

title: Bitcoin Miners Only Hash 80 Bytes
description_body: Only the 80-byte block header is hashed for proof of work. It stores the previous block hash, the merkle root and a nonce.

topic: Myth: mining rewards mean a fixed income
hook: Mining rewards arrive in bitcoin. Your electricity bill doesn't.

scenes.narration: People assume mining rewards are a steady, fixed income.
Rewards are paid in BTC, but electricity and hosting costs are paid in fiat.
So profitability moves with the bitcoin price, and returns are never certain.
Electricity is typically a miner's largest ongoing cost, so check it before anything else.

topic: Myth: the biggest miner always wins the next block
hook: Does the biggest miner win every Bitcoin block? Most people say yes.

scenes.narration: Many people think the miner with the most hashrate wins every block.
Finding a block is a matter of probability. Your chance per block is your share of the total network hashrate.
A bigger share raises your odds, but it never decides any single block.
Even a large miner can go a while without finding one.

title: Myth: The Biggest Miner Always Wins?
description_body: Block finding is probability based. Your chance per block matches your share of network hashrate, and nothing is certain.

hook: One TH/s is a trillion guesses every single second.

scenes.narration: Hashrate is the number of hash attempts a miner makes each second.
One TH/s means one trillion hashes per second.
But it is only a share of the whole network's work, and your chance per block follows that share.
More hashrate also means more electricity, so efficiency in W/TH matters too.

title: What Does 1 TH/s Actually Mean?
description_body: Hashrate counts hash attempts per second, and one TH/s is one trillion of them.

topic: The block reward is the subsidy plus transaction fees
hook: Most people only know half of the Bitcoin block reward.

scenes.narration: The block subsidy is newly created bitcoin. It halves every 210,000 blocks, and became 3.125 BTC in April 2024.
Transaction fees are added to the block's incentive value, so the winning miner earns both.
The miner who adds the next block earns that combined reward.
Only the subsidy follows the halving schedule. Fees are the other part.

title: The Bitcoin Block Reward Has Two Parts
description_body: The block reward combines the newly created subsidy with transaction fees, and the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks.

hook: A digital miner's results can be low or even negative. Here's why.

scenes.narration: Owners are credited daily bitcoin rewards, minus a maintenance charge for electricity and service costs.
Rewards and fees change with the bitcoin price, network difficulty and hashrate.
So net results vary and can be low or negative.
Treat every projection as an estimate, never a promise.

topic: Difficulty can rise 300% or fall 75% in one adjustment
hook: Bitcoin's difficulty can jump 300% in a single adjustment.

scenes.narration: Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks, about two weeks.
At each adjustment it can rise by as much as 300%, or fall by as much as 75%.
The goal is to keep block time near ten minutes.
Higher difficulty means more attempts per block, so miners feel it.

topic: Every full node checks every block itself
hook: Miners can't force Bitcoin to accept a bad block.

scenes.narration: Each full node validates blocks on its own, using the same consensus rules.
Nodes accept a block only if every transaction in it is valid and not already spent.
Finding a valid block is hard, but checking its proof of work is cheap.
Nobody needs to trust a miner's word. The network can check the work.

title: Why Miners Can't Force a Bad Bitcoin Block
description_body: Full nodes validate blocks independently, and proof of work is hard to find but cheap to check.

topic: Beginner guide: why ASICs beat GPUs and CPUs for SHA-256
hook: Why do Bitcoin miners avoid graphics cards entirely?

scenes.narration: An ASIC is a chip built specifically for SHA-256 hashing.
ASICs are far more efficient at it than GPUs or CPUs.
That is why GPU mining Bitcoin is not practical today.
Efficiency is measured in W/TH, and lower means less power per terahash.
